summary: Describes one bandwidth constraints model, called Maximum Allocation, for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. A bandwidth constraints model sets how much of a link each class of traffic may use. This is an experimental specification, not a standard.

eli5.summary: A school bus has seats for everyone, but each class gets its own fixed number of seats that no other class can borrow. This memo describes that kind of seat-limit rule for traffic on a network link.

questions: what is the maximum allocation model
how does mam enforce bandwidth constraints
subtitle: A simple bandwidth allocation rule for traffic classes on network links.

tldr.problem: Diffserv-aware MPLS needs a way to enforce different bandwidth limits for different traffic classes on each link.
tldr.mechanism: The Maximum Allocation Model assigns each class a bandwidth constraint and limits total reservations to the link's maximum. Classes can be isolated from each other or share bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: MAM is simple and intuitive for operators, but cannot simultaneously achieve isolation, bandwidth efficiency, and QoS protection for all traffic classes.

today: RFC 4125 is an Experimental specification. The Maximum Allocation Model is one of three bandwidth constraints models defined for DS-TE; the others are the Russian Doll Model (RFC 4127) and Maximum Allocation with Reservation (RFC 4126). MAM has seen limited deployment in production networks, as many operators prefer the more sophisticated models.

sections.title: Bandwidth Constraints for Multiple Traffic Classes
sections.content:
Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) lets networks separate voice, data, and other traffic into Class-Types (CTs) and give each class different bandwidth limits. A Bandwidth Constraints Model defines the rules for how much bandwidth each class may use.

The Maximum Allocation Model (MAM) is one such model. It is simple: each class has a maximum, and all classes together cannot exceed the link capacity. For example, on a 2.5 Gbps link, voice might be limited to 1 Gbps and data to 2 Gbps, with both together limited to 2.5 Gbps.
sections.eli5: Each type of traffic gets its own bandwidth limit, and the sum of all limits cannot exceed what the link can carry.

sections.title: Maximum Allocation Model Definition
sections.content:
MAM supports up to 8 Class-Types. For each Class-Type c, a bandwidth constraint BCc is configured. The model enforces two rules:

  • Each class's reserved bandwidth must not exceed its constraint: Reserved(CTc) ≤ BCc ≤ Max-Reservable-Bandwidth.
  • The sum of all classes' reserved bandwidth must not exceed the link's maximum: SUM(Reserved(CTc)) ≤ Max-Reservable-Bandwidth.

The sum of the individual constraints may exceed the maximum (SUM(BCc) > Max-Reservable-Bandwidth), allowing classes to share available bandwidth when others are idle. Or the sum may equal the maximum, in which case classes are fully isolated and the second rule never binds.

Both preemption within a class and across classes is allowed. A router implementing MAM must enforce these constraints when admitting new Label Switched Paths (LSPs).
sections.eli5: Two rules: each class stays within its limit, and all classes together stay within the link limit. If the per-class limits add up to more than the link, they can borrow from each other when nobody else needs it.

sections.title: Computing Available Bandwidth
sections.content:
Routers implementing MAM must calculate the unreserved bandwidth for each Traffic Engineering Class before admitting a new LSP. The unreserved bandwidth for TE-Class i is the minimum of:

  • The bandwidth constraint of its class minus the reserved bandwidth in that class (for the requesting priority level).
  • The link maximum minus all reserved bandwidth (for the requesting priority level and all lower-priority levels).

This ensures that an LSP cannot exceed either its class limit or the overall link limit. The exact formula depends on the preemption priority requested by the LSP and the priorities of existing LSPs in that class.

The details of the admission control algorithm are outside the scope of the specification, but the example formula reflects how the two constraints interact to determine whether an LSP can be admitted.
sections.eli5: Before admitting a new connection, check if it fits within both its class limit and the link total. Whichever is tighter wins.

sections.title: Scenario Examples
sections.content:
Scenario 1: Limiting Voice sets voice (CT1) to a fixed percentage, data (CT0) to the full capacity or a specific limit, and the link maximum to full capacity. Voice LSPs are configured with preemption priority 0 and data with priority 1, so voice can preempt. DS-TE ensures voice is limited, data uses the rest, and voice traffic can push out data.

Scenario 2: Maintaining Proportions allocates voice 45%, premium data 35%, and best-effort 100% (unused portion) of the link. Preemption priorities are assigned per class. The model guarantees that each class stays within its proportion, regardless of the order LSPs are routed or which preemption levels are used, and even during failures.

Scenario 3: Guaranteed Services reserves a fixed percentage for a guaranteed service and lets other traffic use remaining capacity. MAM ensures the guaranteed service meets its QoS objectives while allowing full utilization of spare bandwidth.
sections.eli5: Three examples show voice capped at 1 Gbps while data uses the rest; three classes each getting their proportional share; and a premium service getting guaranteed bandwidth while others compete for the rest.

sections.title: Strengths and Limitations
sections.content:
MAM is attractive because network operators find it simple and intuitive, it matches basic bandwidth control policies, it can isolate classes from each other, and it protects premium classes against QoS degradation. MAM requires only limited protocol extensions.

However, MAM cannot simultaneously achieve isolation, efficiency, and QoS protection for non-premium classes. Under overload, lower-class traffic may suffer even though they are within their allocated bandwidth, because the overall link is congested. The Russian Doll Model (RFC 4127) and Maximum Allocation with Reservation (RFC 4126) offer alternatives with different trade-offs.
sections.eli5: MAM is easy to understand and use, good at protecting important traffic, but it does not always share bandwidth as well as fancier models when the network gets busy.
